items.context:
A 200-line pipeline written as one function returns a per-fault summary
table, and one column of it looks wrong.

What does writing it as a single function cost you here?
items.why:
A pipeline built from stages has a seam at every boundary: you can open
the output of load, of clean, of aggregate, and see exactly what each one
produced. One long function has no such seam, so every question about the
middle costs you a full re-run with prints added.
items.true: There is no intermediate output to open, so you cannot tell which step introduced it without adding prints and re-running the whole thing
false: Nothing; one function is easier to debug because all the logic sits in one place
The error has to be in the aggregation, since that is the last step that ran
You can only find it by rewriting the pipeline in Polars, whose query plan shows each step

items.context:
A Polars pipeline starts with `pl.scan_parquet(...)` and later selects 6 of
a table's 55 columns before `.collect()`.

What does the plan do with that, and what is the idea called?
items.why:
Because scan_parquet builds a plan instead of reading immediately, a
later `.select()` folds back into the read itself, so the columns you
never asked for are never pulled off disk. This is the same saving
DuckDB applied to Parquet in Lecture 4, now inside a dataframe pipeline
with no server involved.
items.true: It folds the selection into the scan, so only those 6 columns are read off disk: projection pushdown
false: Nothing; scan_parquet always reads every column regardless of what is selected later
It reads all 55 columns into memory first, then drops 49 of them: eager projection
It reads only the first 6 columns in file order, which only works if you select by position

items.context: What does lazy evaluation cost you, in Polars?
items.why:
A malformed expression may not raise until `.collect()`, several lines
and possibly several stages from the mistake, where pandas' eager default
would have failed right on the offending line. That debugging cost is
real, and it is why an exploratory notebook often stays eager.
items.true: Errors move away from the line that causes them, sometimes several stages away
false: Memory, since the whole plan must be held before anything executes
Determinism, since the optimizer may reorder operations between runs
Type safety, since column types are only known once the data is materialized

items.context: When is staying with pandas the right call, even though Polars is faster?
items.why:
Polars is stricter, and stricter costs you while you are still learning
it: more of your mistakes become real errors instead of quiet
workarounds. Stay with pandas when your codebase or collaborators only
speak it; reach for Polars when a run gets slow enough to interrupt your
work. Note the
last option is wrong for the same reason converting is cheap: shared
Arrow layout, so plotting from a Polars result costs little.
items.true: When your codebase or your collaborators only speak pandas
false: When the data fits in memory, since Polars' advantage only appears above that
When the transformations are simple, since Polars' planner needs complex queries to pay off
When you need plotting, since Polars cannot be converted to a plottable form

items.context:
A pipeline stage caches its output to Parquet under a name that mentions
only the stage, `clean.parquet`. A config parameter the stage depends on
changes, and the stage is re-run.

What happens?
items.why:
Naming the cache after the stage rather than after the inputs and
settings that actually determine its contents is the trap. The fix is
to name the cached file after the config too, not just the stage, so a
changed setting produces a different filename and the old one is never
mistaken for current.
items.true: The stale file is reused silently, because nothing about the filename reflects the config
false: The cache is invalidated automatically, since the config is part of the stage's inputs
The stage fails, since the cached schema no longer matches the new config
A new cache entry is written alongside the old one, and the newer is preferred

items.context:
A Python loop over a sensor column, against the same test done on the
whole column at once.

Before you look: how much slower is the loop?
items.why:
Measured on this session's reactor-pressure column, 480,000 readings:
the whole-column comparison takes 0.2 ms, a plain `for` loop takes about
20 ms, and the same thing written with `iterrows()` takes about 3,900 ms.
The whole-column version hands the work to compiled code once; the loop
pays Python's per-row cost 480,000 times. Which loop you write matters
as much as whether you write one.
items.true: Hundreds of times slower, and thousands of times if you write it with `iterrows()`
false: About 5 times slower, which is the usual interpreter overhead
Roughly the same, since NumPy loops internally anyway
Slower only past a few million rows; at this size it makes little difference

items.context: Converting a table from pandas to Polars, or back, is usually cheap. Why?
items.why:
Arrow is the columnar format for data held in memory, Parquet's
counterpart from Lecture 4 on disk. Because pandas and Polars both lay
their columns out in Arrow, moving a table between the two is cheap,
which is what makes prototyping in whichever one you know a reasonable
default.
items.true: Both lay their columns out the same way in memory, the Arrow format
false: Both libraries call the same C extension underneath, so no data actually moves
pandas and Polars use identical column names and types by convention, so no translation is needed
Polars automatically caches every pandas dataframe it has already seen

items.context:
What does it mean for a pipeline stage to be idempotent, and why does it
matter?
items.why:
Retryability is the whole payoff. You do not need to know whether the
last attempt finished; you just run the stage again. That is what a
database's transactions gave you for free, and what a plain Python
pipeline has to rebuild by hand.
items.true: Running it twice has the same effect as running it once, so a partial failure can be retried without corrupting anything
false: It runs in constant time regardless of input size, which makes scheduling predictable
It holds no state between invocations, so stages can run in any order
It writes atomically, so a reader never sees a half-written file

items.context:
Open [`l05-pipelines.ipynb`](../lectures/l05/l05-pipelines.ipynb) and run
the pandas-against-Polars benchmark on the sensor data.

What should you conclude from whichever number you get?
items.why:
A speed ratio measured on one laptop, one dataset, and one set of
operations does not generalize to your own pipeline. The number worth
carrying from this session is the hundredfold vectorization gap, not
this ratio, because that one is about the shape of the computation
rather than about which library you chose.
items.true: That the ratio is a property of this workload and this machine, and the transferable habit is measuring rather than assuming
false: That Polars should replace pandas in your projects, since the benchmark settles it
That the two are equivalent, since the difference is within run-to-run noise
That benchmarks of this kind are not meaningful, since real pipelines are dominated by input and output
